data.title: Uti expects $925M-$945M fiscal 2027 revenue while targeting 34,000-35,500 starts
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: Universal Technical Institute (UTI) Q4 fiscal 2026

Management View

  • "We finished fiscal 2026 with our North Star strategy on track" and "we remain confident that we will exceed $1.2 billion in revenue and approach $220 million in adjusted EBITDA in fiscal 2029" (CEO Jerome Grant).
  • "Revenue grew 7% year-over-year to $897 million" and "starts came in below where we wanted them to be" even as "in the quarter, we still grew by 3% year-over-year" (CEO Grant).
  • "We're confident that the changes and enhancements we have implemented have fixed the high school admissions issue" and "our goal is to add up to 1,000 seats to existing programs by the end of fiscal 2027" (CEO Grant).
  • "We're also taking modest pricing actions on our skilled trade programs" and "today, we're introducing the next generation of UTI campuses" called "Skilled Trades Max" (CEO Grant).
  • "Fourth quarter revenue on a consolidated basis increased 6% to $235.9 million" and "consolidated net income for the fourth quarter was $18.0 million or $0.32 per diluted share" (Executive VP & CFO Bruce Schuman).
  • "In August, we signed a new $200 million revolving credit facility, up from $125 million" and "we have more than sufficient resources to fund the remainder of North Star Phase 2 without the need for any new financing" (CFO Schuman).

Outlook

  • "For fiscal 2027, we expect new student starts of 34,000 to 35,500" and "we expect revenue of $925 million to $945 million this year" (CFO Schuman).
  • "The softer Q4 2026 cohort creates a lower entering student population for fiscal 2027 and therefore, moderates near-term revenue growth" and "this is the dynamic in our student base specific to fiscal 2026 and fiscal 2027" (CFO Schuman).
  • "The revenue outlook this year, combined with planned growth investments as well as the onetime integration and restructuring costs" is expected to result in "a net income outlook of $0 to $5 million for the year" and "diluted earnings per share of $0.00 to $0.09" (CFO Schuman).
  • "Baseline adjusted EBITDA is expected to be $135 million to $141 million" and "we expect reported adjusted EBITDA to be between $100 million and $106 million" (CFO Schuman).
  • "We expect to execute on $160 million to $170 million of capital expenditures in fiscal 2027" (CFO Schuman).

Financial Results

  • "Fourth quarter revenue on a consolidated basis increased 6% to $235.9 million" with "Concorde" at "$82.2 million" and "the UTI division" at "$153.6 million" (CFO Schuman).
  • "For the full year, consolidated revenue grew 7.4% to $897 million" with "Concorde" at "$319.8 million" and "the UTI division" at "$577.2 million" (CFO Schuman).
  • "Consolidated net income for the fourth quarter was $18.0 million" and "$33.6 million" for the full year (CFO Schuman).
  • "Baseline adjusted EBITDA was $49.5 million for the fourth quarter and $136.6 million for the full year" while "our SEC reported adjusted EBITDA was $42.5 million for the fourth quarter and $102 million for the full year" (CFO Schuman).
  • "For the year, capital expenditures were $112.9 million" and "total available liquidity at the end of the year was $321 million" (CFO Schuman).

Q&A

  • Steven Frankel, Rosenblatt: Asked how starts growth can be modest if skilled trades demand is seat-constrained and whether there is deceleration in auto/diesel; CEO Grant: "the softness we saw in the fourth quarter was highly concentrated to auto diesel" and "that's why we've enhanced our growth agenda to focus also on creating 1,000 new seats of capacity".
  • Steven Frankel, Rosenblatt: Asked about pulling missed high school students into the December quarter; CEO Grant: "we're not reporting on the first quarter right now" and "we'll report on that when we do the first quarter".
  • Steven Frankel, Rosenblatt: Asked about replicating the Heartland co-branded model to reduce capital intensity; CEO Grant: "we're in deep conversations with them and other parties" including "things like HVAC and aviation".
  • Eric Martinuzzi, Lake Street: Asked whether mix shift toward shorter skilled trades pressures margins and FY29 EBITDA margin; CEO Grant: "as we scale up these businesses and create capacity on it, that margin gap will shrink" and "our confidence hasn't wavered" on "approaching $220 million in EBITDA".
  • Griffin Boss, B. Riley: Asked why midpoint revenue growth lags starts growth in FY27 guidance; CFO Schuman: "that is really the only disconnect" and "it is that carry-in issue from the Q4".
  • Jasper Bibb, Truist: Pressed on higher FY27 CapEx and whether builds are more capital intensive; CFO Schuman: "fundamentally, it's really a timing issue" and "the vast majority is growth" ("50%" new campuses, "over 15%" replications/new programs, and "a full 10%" skilled trades expansions).
  • Jasper Bibb, Truist: Asked about buybacks vs. growth spend; CEO Grant: "we're staying the course" and "'26 and '27 were going to be significant investment years to load the machine for '28 and '29".
  • Mike Grondahl, Northland: Asked about auto/diesel utilization and repurposing space; CEO Grant: "we're 40% to 50% capacity in our auto diesel" and "we're thinking very deeply about how we reimagine how auto diesel is being taught".

Sentiment Analysis

  • Analysts: slightly negative to pressing, with repeated probing on the Q4 high school/auto-diesel shortfall, the starts-to-revenue bridge, and elevated CapEx (e.g., "I'm just trying to square in my mind" and "I'm just kind of struggling to bridge" from Steven Frankel and Jasper Bibb).
  • Management: slightly positive and corrective in tone, emphasizing fixes and long-term targets (e.g., "we believe we've corrected course" and "our confidence hasn't wavered" from CEO Grant; "that is really the only disconnect" from CFO Schuman).
  • Versus last quarter: management messaging shifted from identifying execution issues to asserting remediation progress (Q4: "fixed the high school admissions issue"; Q3: "we have unfortunately seen some near-term softness" and "we are proactively taking steps").

Quarter-over-Quarter Comparison

  • High school channel: Q3 flagged execution shortfalls ("we simply did not get to all the prospective students") while Q4 asserted remediation ("our UTI high school admissions team is now fully staffed" and "high school presentations and enrollments for 2027 fall term are already significantly up").
  • Capacity constraints: Q4 introduced a quantified near-term capacity target ("add up to 1,000 seats") and operational tactics ("we're offering welding sections after midnight"), expanding beyond Q3’s focus on improving execution and ongoing capacity work.
  • Investment cadence: Q3 guided FY26 revenue "$893 million to $900 million" and reported adjusted EBITDA "$100 million to $103 million"; Q4 finalized FY26 at "$897 million" and "$102 million" and set FY27 CapEx at "$160 million to $170 million".
  • Strategy detail: Q4 added the "Skilled Trades Max" campus model and explicitly laid out "4 more" campuses in FY27 and plans to open "4 more" in each of FY28 and FY29.

Risks and Concerns

  • "Personnel challenges in our high school admissions channel" and "capacity constraints" were cited as factors that "put a damper on our Q4 2026 performance" (CEO Grant).
  • "The softer Q4 2026 cohort creates a lower entering student population for fiscal 2027" (CFO Schuman).
  • "On the marketing side, the shift towards zero-click search and AI-driven discovery requires continued investment" (CEO Grant).
  • "Onetime integration and restructuring costs to unify and simplify the company and move to a single operating structure" were included in FY27 outlook (CFO Schuman).

Final Takeaway

Management framed fiscal 2026 as a growth-and-investment year that still produced $897 million in revenue and set up an FY27 plan centered on rebuilding high school admissions execution, adding up to 1,000 incremental skilled-trades seats by the end of FY27, and funding a heavier build cycle. The company’s FY27 outlook called for 34,000 to 35,500 starts and $925 million to $945 million revenue, while reiterating longer-term North Star targets to exceed $1.2 billion in revenue and approach $220 million in adjusted EBITDA by fiscal 2029.

data.title: U.S. oil price slides as data shows larger-than-expected increases in crude, gasoline stocks
data.description:
Crude oil futures fell Wednesday as the market continued to focus more on strong supply than on the conflict in the Middle East.

Oil was part of a broad retreat across commodities as the dollar strengthened to a fresh 19-month high, creating a headwind for raw materials priced in the currency.

The Brent crude benchmark has retreated by more than 20% so far this month, as supplies from the Middle East recovered and President Trump held off on renewed large-scale strikes against Iran, although low-level fighting has flared up across the region recently.

While recovering Middle East supply keeps crude under pressure, continued attacks on vessels around the Strait of Hormuz and renewed strikes on Persian Gulf infrastructure "highlight the fragility of this recovery," Sparta Commodities oil analyst Abhishek Kumar said in a note.

Russian refining is still disrupted by Ukrainian attacks, with crude exports rising as refinery outages limit domestic processing, developments that "continue to support a geopolitical premium in European diesel despite the broader weakness in crude," Kumar added.

The decline in U.S. crude futures was exacerbated by the U.S. Energy Information Administration's weekly report showing larger-than-expected increases in crude oil and gasoline inventories, adding to expectations of a supply surplus.

U.S. commercial crude oil stocks excluding the Strategic Petroleum Reserve rose by 3.4M barrels to 417.8M in the week ended November 13 and were 3% below the five-year average for the time of year, according to the EIA.

U.S. gasoline inventories increased by 5.2M barrels to 215.9M barrels and were 3% above the five-year average for the time of year, and distillate fuel stocks rose by 1.6M barrels to 104.9M barrels and were 7% below the five-year average for the time of year, the EIA said.

The stock builds added to selling pressure, Gelber & Associates analysts said, adding, "Attacks involving Iran and commercial shipping ​still threaten deliveries through the Strait of Hormuz, but those risks have provided limited support against the growing expectation of a global surplus."

On Wednesday, front-month Nymex crude (CL1:COM) for December delivery fell 3.2% to $83.26/bbl, its lowest settlement value since August 26, and front-month Brent crude (CO1:COM) for January delivery slipped 1.3% to $91.95/bbl, its lowest close since November 10.

Additionally, front-month Nymex December natural gas (NG1:COM) rose 5.1% to $3.372/MMBtu, its best settlement value since February 6, as cooler weather forecasts improved the near-term demand outlook.

data.title: Venture Global CEO sees final investment decisions on two key projects in next year's H1
data.description:
Venture Global's (VG) growth plans have progressed well, and the company intends to make final investment decisions for the expansion of its CP2 and Plaquemines projects in next year's H1, and some equipment orders have already been placed, CEO Michael Sabel told The Wall Street Journal in an interview Wednesday.

Venture Global (VG) is advancing the two expansion projects to push its liquefied natural gas production capacity past 100M metric tons/year before the end of 2030.

The expansion at CP2 is expected to provide an additional 10M tons/year of LNG, and the Plaquemines expansion should increase production by 7M-8M tons/year.

LNG suppliers and analysts are split between those that forecast an impending supply glut once energy markets stabilize and those that expect demand will continue to rise, but Sabel told WSJ that the company does not believe there is a supply glut.

Instead, Venture Global (VG) expects a small LNG shortage heading into the early 2030s with large supply projects likely to run behind schedule, Sabel said.

The outlook is also clouded by questions over when lost volumes from Qatar will return to the market, as damage to the country's facilities from the Middle East conflict has cut the country’s export capacity by ~17%.

data.title: Wheat leads U.S. grain futures lower, falling to lowest since January
data.description:
CBOT December wheat futures fell $0.25 to $5.70 per bushel on Wednesday, the contract's lowest level since January, leading the market lower as part of a broad selloff in commodities.

The dollar rallied to a 19-month high on rising expectations for an interest rate hike next month, which could further weigh on demand by making U.S. grains less competitive in the global market.

Overall commodity sentiment is in a state of deflation, Gary Sandlund of Futures International said in a note, pointing to sharp declines in oil and gold, "just to name a few," while geopolitical tensions seem to be the "new normal" and markets have adapted to it.

U.S. wheat prices had gained in the previous session after a Ukrainian attack destroyed parts of the Crimea bridge, threatening further disruption to Russian wheat exports.

"Shipments have already been effectively nonexistent relative to pre-war norms, but this damage could mean a substantial delay to resumed commodity flow even if an agreement was somehow reached," Mike Castle of StoneX wrote.

The market also continues to wonder whether China will agree to buy U.S. corn when Presidents Trump and Xi meet this week, as analysts say export demand remains a central focus for the corn market following its sluggish start to the marketing year.

CBOT wheat (W_1:COM) for December delivery plunged 4.2% to $5.70 per bushel, corn (C_1:COM) for December delivery dropped 2.5% to $4.35 1/2 per bushel, and January soybean (S_1:COM) slipped 0.7% to 12.16 3/4 per bushel.

data.title: Sanofi wins approval of venglustat for Gaucher disease
data.description:
• The US FDA approved Sanofi's (SNY) Infilbray (venglustat) for neurological manifestations of Type 3 Gaucher disease.
  • Approval was based on data from the phase 3 LEAP2MONO study that found venglustat led to improvements in neurological manifestations better than the enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) imiglucerase.
  • The drug's label carries warnings for suicidal ideation and behavior, lens opacification in pediatric patients, and embryofoetal toxicity.
  • Infilbray is an oral, glucosylceramide synthase inhibitor. Sanofi said it would pursue additional approvals for the treatment in other countries this year and in 2027.

data.title: Gold and silver sink to 14-month lows as hawkish Fed commentary boosts dollar
data.description:
Gold and silver futures fell Wednesday to their lowest levels since September 2025, pressured by a stronger dollar and expectations of further interest rate hikes before year-end by the U.S. Federal Reserve.

Gold dropped more than 3% and broke below $3,750/oz, while silver suffered even larger losses as concerns about industrial demand and tighter financial conditions compounded the selloff.

The release of hawkish minutes from the Fed's October meeting reinforced expectations for additional monetary tightening, indicating the central bank remains firmly committed to raising interest rates to bring inflation down to its 2% target.

The minutes echoed comments from ​Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller, who said the Fed needs to "shock people" as prices continue to rise more than he expected by either ⁠approving a 50-basis point rate hike in December or communicating a faster pace of rate increases in 2027.

The dollar strengthened to a fresh 19-month high on Wednesday, as the hawkish commentary and recent economic data solidified expectations for ​a rate hike next month.

"The selloff is being driven by hawkish Fed commentary pointing to the need for several additional rate hikes before spring to contain stubborn inflation, alongside continued dollar strength and real yields at multi-decade highs," Saxo Bank analysts said in a note.

Gold and silver are also getting dragged down in part by the slide in copper (HG1:COM), which plunged more than 5% on Comex to $5.6595/lb, its lowest settlement since April 7.

"Copper is getting hit hard, and the weakness is spilling across the complex," squeezed by worries about AI investment prospects, the Chinese demand outlook, and uncertainty around U.S. trade policy, Phil Flynn of Price Futures Group said.

"A firmer dollar and expectations that interest rates may stay higher are weighing on gold and silver, while momentum selling is adding pressure," Flynn added.

On Wednesday, front-month Comex gold (XAUUSD:CUR) for November delivery plunged 3.1% to $3,736.80/oz, and front-month Comex November silver (XAGUSD:CUR) slumped 4.8% to $44.999/oz, the lowest settlement for the respective metals since September 24 and 25, 2025.
